Establishment
ess-TAB-lish-ment
n. (the act of establishing; a settled or confirmed state)
Latin stabilire, to make firm, from stabilis, stable, through French establir. In 2 Chronicles 32:1 it denotes the settled state of Hezekiah's reformation.

Definition · Webster 1828 · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

The Chronicler sets Sennacherib's invasion immediately after Hezekiah's reforms, and the joint is one word: “After these things, and the establishment thereof, Sennacherib king of Assyria came, and entered into Judah, and encamped against the fenced cities, and thought to win them for himself” (2 Chronicles 32:1). These things are the cleansing of the temple, the restored passover, the smashed images, the reorganised priesthood. The establishment thereof means that the reformation held; it was not a gesture but a settled state. And then the Assyrian came. The Authorized Version uses establishment once. The dictionary notes carefully what the verse does not teach: that reformation purchases peace. Hezekiah did right and was invaded. What the reformation purchased was a king who could say the right thing when the invasion came: “With him is an arm of flesh; but with us is the LORD our God to help us, and to fight our battles” (2 Chronicles 32:8). A church that has settled its doctrine before the trial arrives has not bought immunity; it has bought the ability to stand. The establishment of the reformation and the coming of Sennacherib belong in the same verse on purpose.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828): ESTABLISHMENT, noun The act of establishing, founding, ratifying or ordaining; settlement; fixed state.

expand to see more

ESTABLISHMENT, noun The act of establishing, founding, ratifying or ordaining.

2. Settlement; fixed state.

3. Confirmation; ratification of what has been settled or made.

4. Settled regulation; form; ordinance; system of laws; constitution of government.

5. That which is fixed or established; as a permanent civil or military force.

Key Scripture

2Ch 32:1 — "After these things, and the establishment thereof, Sennacherib king of Assyria came, and entered into Judah, and encamped against the fenced cities, and thought to win them for himself."

2Ch 32:8 — "With him is an arm of flesh; but with us is the LORD our God to help us, and to fight our battles. And the people rested themselves upon the words of Hezekiah king of Judah."

2Ch 31:21 — "And in every work that he began in the service of the house of God, and in the law, and in the commandments, to seek his God, he did it with all his heart, and prospered."

Modern Corruption

Obedience is widely preached as a guarantee of ease; 2 Chronicles 32:1 puts the invasion immediately after the reformation held.

expand to see more

The prosperity reading cannot handle this verse. Hezekiah had done every work in the service of the house of God with all his heart, and the next sentence is Sennacherib encamping against the fenced cities. Scripture joins the two deliberately. Obedience is not a transaction, and the Chronicler's commendation of Hezekiah is not undone by the siege.

The principle to recover is what establishment is actually for. Because the reformation had settled, Hezekiah knew what to say when the Assyrian came, and the people rested themselves upon his words. Doctrine settled in peacetime is what a people stand on in war.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

From Latin stabilire, to make firm; in 2 Chronicles 32:1 the settled state of Hezekiah's reformation, immediately before the siege.

expand to see more

Latin stabilis, firm; stabilire, to make firm; French establir.

2 Chronicles 32:1 is the only place the Authorized Version uses establishment.

These things are Hezekiah's reforms; the establishment thereof is their holding.

Sennacherib came after the reformation, not before it.

2 Chronicles 31:21 is the Chronicler's verdict: he did it with all his heart, and prospered.
